The big idea

Source: vignettes/big-idea.Rmd
big-idea.Rmd
library(csvschema)

A CSV forgets everything but the text. csvschema keeps the schema with the data by borrowing the trick the internet uses to move data over an unreliable network: cut the thing into small, self-checking packets, send many copies by different routes, and reassemble whatever arrives — verifying at the end that the reassembled whole is the right one.

This article shows the idea end to end on a tiny example.

1. A little data

We use four columns of the built-in dg_states table.

head(dg_states[, c("state", "region", "population", "south")])
#>        state region population south
#> 1    Alabama  South       3615  TRUE
#> 2     Alaska   West        365 FALSE
#> 3    Arizona   West       2212 FALSE
#> 4   Arkansas  South       2110  TRUE
#> 5 California   West      21198 FALSE
#> 6   Colorado   West       2541 FALSE

2. Its schema

cs_schema() reads the column classes into a schema. It is exactly a Frictionless Table Schema — types, the factor’s categories, the key:

ex <- dg_states[, c("state", "region", "population", "south")]
s <- cs_schema(ex, primary_key = "state")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(cs_schema_to_frictionless(s), pretty = TRUE,
                     auto_unbox = TRUE))
#> {
#>   "fields": [
#>     {
#>       "name": "state",
#>       "type": "string"
#>     },
#>     {
#>       "name": "region",
#>       "type": "string",
#>       "categories": [
#>         "Northeast",
#>         "South",
#>         "North Central",
#>         "West"
#>       ]
#>     },
#>     {
#>       "name": "population",
#>       "type": "number"
#>     },
#>     {
#>       "name": "south",
#>       "type": "boolean"
#>     }
#>   ],
#>   "primaryKey": [
#>     "state"
#>   ]
#> }

3. The schema as packets

cs_packetize() atomizes that schema into short ASCII tokens. Each is one unquoted CSV cell: a type-and-index id, the payload, and a CRC-32, wrapped in {{ }}. Packet S0 is the header (it carries the whole-schema hash); S1–S4 are the fields; the last is the table packet with the primary key.

writeLines(cs_packetize(s))
#> {{S0/6~cs=1^enc=utf-8^dialect=rfc4180^fields=4^rows=50^mtu=200^hash=458d22e11e1f~6e108055}}
#> {{S1/6~state^str~976d416d}}
#> {{S2/6~region^str^lev=Northeast!South!North+Central!West~cce9247d}}
#> {{S3/6~population^num~16a4103f}}
#> {{S4/6~south^bool~4c713ce3}}
#> {{S5/6~pk=state~87e2751a}}

These packets are then copied and spread across the rows of a _schema column. Any surviving subset of rows that contains one copy of each is enough to rebuild the schema.

The internet metaphor

The design separates the same three problems TCP/IP does, and solves two of them the same way. The third it cannot, so it does something else.

1. Fragmentation metadata — which piece, and how many?

An IP fragment carries an identification number, an offset, and a more-fragments flag. A csvschema packet carries S<k>/<P>: the index k and the total P (in every packet, so losing the last one is still detectable). The “identification” that groups a set is the whole-schema hash in packet S0.

2. Per-piece integrity — is this piece intact?

Every IP/TCP/UDP header has a checksum; Ethernet frames a CRC-32. The receiver recomputes it and, on a mismatch, discards the piece. A csvschema packet ends with a CRC-32 over its id~payload. On read, a packet that fails is dropped exactly as if its row had been deleted:

pk <- cs_packetize(s)
tampered <- pk[3]
substr(tampered, 12, 12) <- "X"          # a spreadsheet, or find-and-replace
parsed <- cs_parse_packets(c(pk[3], tampered))
parsed[, c("type", "index", "crc_ok")]
#>   type index crc_ok
#> 1    s     2   TRUE
#> 2    s     2  FALSE

The garbled copy is the dead end in the diagram; the intact copy carries the same packet, so the schema still rebuilds. Because the packet column holds many copies, the few that die do not matter:

# the real file keeps lots of copies, so recovery is unaffected
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
cs_write(ex, tmp, sidecar = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
cs_report(cs_read_csv(tmp, verbose = FALSE))$status
#> [1] "verified"

3. Whole-object verification — is the reassembled thing the right thing?

A BitTorrent client checks each piece and an info-hash over the whole file, so pieces collected from many peers still assemble into exactly the published file. Packet S0 carries a hash over the canonical schema text; cs_recover() recomputes it after reassembly. A mismatch means version mixing — two different schemas were bound together — and is reported, not accepted.

Is the corruption check the handshake?

Not quite — and the difference is the whole point.

TCP’s handshake and its resend of garbled datagrams (the loop in the classic diagram) need a two-way conversation: the receiver tells the sender what arrived, and the sender retransmits the rest. A CSV file is a one-way broadcast — it is read long after it was written, by someone who cannot ask for a resend.

So csvschema keeps only the halves of the idea that work without a back-channel:

  • The CRC-32 on each packet is the per-datagram checksum — it detects a garbled packet and drops it. That is the “is this piece intact?” check, not a handshake.
  • With no way to request a resend, it sends many copies up front instead — forward error correction by repetition, like PAR2 blocks for Usenet or the redundancy in a QR code. The redundancy math sizes how many copies survive a given fraction of row loss.
  • The whole-schema hash is the final “is this the right thing?” check, like BitTorrent’s info-hash.

Detection and redundancy, computed once and frozen into the file; no conversation required.
